title: Hidden health risks of traditional fall family activities
summary:
Title: Hidden health risks of traditional fall family activities

Published Time: 2026-11-02T05:05:00.000Z

The most dangerous thing at a pumpkin patch may not be the pumpkin. And the greatest health risk at an apple orchard may have nothing to do with the apples.

It could be the pony your child rides. The goat they pet. The hamburger cooked on a makeshift grill. Or the shared barrel of water where children take turns bobbing for apples.

These are the experiences that make fall traditions memorable. But they can also introduce risks involving animal-borne pathogens, contaminated surfaces, unsafe food handling, and inadequate sanitation.

For most families, a day at the farm ends with photographs and happy memories. For others, exposure to an invisible pathogen can mean an emergency room, kidney failure, or worse.

Young children, older adults, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems can face particularly serious consequences.

The problem is not that pumpkin patches and apple orchards are inherently unsafe. It is that we have spent decades celebrating these family traditions without consistently recognizing the public health responsibilities that come with them.

And as a developing E. coli investigation in California reminds us, those responsibilities are far from theoretical.

**A pumpkin patch is rarely just a pumpkin patch**  
In San Luis Obispo County, CA, public health officials are investigating five cases of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and a possible connection to Brookshire Farms, a seasonal agricultural attraction. Several children have reportedly experienced severe illness.

The farm voluntarily closed and has cooperated with investigators. The source of the infections has not been established.

The European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) reported the distribution of gummies containing THC, the main psychoactive substance in cannabis, sold in counterfeit packs of an unnamed but well-known European brand.

Published Time: 2026-11-02T05:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
## Subscribe to Food Safety News

A Salmonella outbreak in the United Kingdom linked to eggs from Ukraine has sickened almost 80 people across two years.

The strain is associated with 40 illnesses in England in 2026 and 36 in 2025.

As part of a large Salmonella Enteritidis outbreak with 700 patients connected to imported eggs, microbiological testing of nearly 3,000 eggs was undertaken by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). This sampling detected Salmonella Enteritidis in a batch of eggs from Ukraine and a separate outbreak.

Affected eggs came from Yasensvit and are stamped with the code 3UA1012066. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) and Food Standards Scotland (FSS) asked businesses to stop using them.

Yasensvit, part of the Ovostar Union Group, is one of the largest producers of eggs and egg products in Europe and operates in international markets. The company [previously urged people](https://www.foodsafetynews.com/2026/10/ukrainian-egg-firm-comments-on-uk-salmonella-link/) to avoid drawing what it called “premature conclusions” until all the facts were established.

**Detection of Salmonella**  
In October, Salmonella Enteritidis was detected in three samples of six pooled eggs each from the Ukrainian producer. Nine isolates were sent to the reference laboratory and it was confirmed via whole genome sequencing (WGS) that they were the same strain of Salmonella Enteritidis and associated with human infections.

The date of sampling was Sept. 23, 2026. Eggs were reportedly laid and packaged on Aug. 23, with an expiry date of Sept. 19. This means samples were taken four days after the best before date.

Title: Fraud alerts at steady levels in Europe; 13 alerts mention the United States

URL Source: https://www.foodsafetynews.com/2026/10/fraud-alerts-at-steady-levels-in-europe-13-alerts-mention-the-united-states/

Published Time: 2026-10-30T04:01:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Plus: Changes to U.S. meat exports to the EU

![Image 1: Fraud alerts at steady levels in Europe; 13 alerts mention the United States](https://storage.ghost.io/c/43/4e/434e508a-5e2f-4102-a53d-00bca10bb4bf/content/images/size/w30/2026/10/food-fraud-adulteration-authenticity-1.png)

Published:October 30, 2026, 12:01 am

Potential fraud and non-compliance cases discussed between European countries remained stable in September, as supplements continued to dominate.

Thirteen alerts mentioned the United States in September. The majority were related to supplements. Other notices were for sodium benzoate in soft and energy drinks and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) in sweets.
